Alright, the binary build looks solid – I successfully compiled glint, installed it to ~/.local/bin, and verified its headless functionality with a prompt. The next logical step is to ensure that the interactive TUI, now that it’s a compiled binary, behaves the same as the development version. Specifically, I want to test the diagnostics opt‑out feature (`/no-diagnostics`) and then re‑enable diagnostics with `/diagnostics`. 

Why is this important? The earlier interactive tests were run via the source code (`bun run ...`). Those runs automatically include the Ink devtools import chain, which we had to resolve by adding `react-devtools-core`. Now that the binary is self‑contained, I need to confirm that the runtime commands still work and that the diagnostics toggling actually suppresses and then restores the diagnostic output. This will also verify that the `/no-diagnostics` command correctly sets the internal flag and that the subsequent `/diagnostics` command clears it.

To capture the TUI output reliably, I’ll use tmux. It lets me start a detached session, run the binary, send keystrokes, and then capture the pane contents. I should clean up any existing `glint` session first to avoid interference, so I’ll start with `tmux kill-session -t glint`. Then I’ll create a new session named `glint`, set a reasonable size (`-x 100 -y 32`) for readability, and set the working directory to `/tmp/glint-test` where the test files live. I’ll launch the binary with `--no-intro` to skip the logo animation and speed up the test, redirecting any TUI errors to a temp log just in case.

After launching, I need a short pause (`sleep 2`) to give the TUI time to initialize. Then I’ll send the `/no-diagnostics` command. In Ink/TUI, commands are entered by typing a slash followed by the command and pressing Enter. I’ll use `tmux send-keys -t glint '/no-diagnostics'` and then a separate `Enter` keystroke. A brief `sleep 0.3` after sending the command should let the UI process it. 

Next, I’ll wait another second to let any diagnostic suppression take effect, then send the `/diagnostics` command in the same way, again followed by `Enter` and a short pause. Finally, after another second for the UI to reflect the re‑enabled diagnostics, I’ll capture the pane contents with `tmux capture-pane -t glint -p`, filter out blank lines (`grep -v '^\\s*$'`), and take the last 14 lines (`tail -14`) to see the relevant output – this should include confirmation messages about diagnostics being turned off and on, and possibly some diagnostic logs that appear after re‑enabling.

Putting it all together, the full bash command sequence will be:
1. Kill any existing `glint` tmux session.
2. Start a new detached session running `glint --no-intro`.
3. Sleep 2 seconds.
4. Send `/no-diagnostics` and press Enter.
5. Sleep 0.3 seconds.
6. Send `/diagnostics` and press Enter.
7. Sleep 1 second.
8. Capture and filter the pane output.

That sequence directly addresses the need to verify diagnostics toggling in the compiled TUI, using the same pattern I’ve employed for previous tmux‑based UI checks. I’ll now issue this as a Bash tool call with an appropriate description.

arguments.command: tmux kill-session -t glint 2>/dev/null; tmux new-session -d -s glint -x 100 -y 32 -c /tmp/glint-test 'glint --no-intro 2>/tmp/glint-tui-err.log' && sleep 2 && tmux send-keys -t glint '/no-diagnostics' && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t glint Enter && sleep 1 && tmux send-keys -t glint '/diagnostics' && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t glint Enter && sleep 1 && tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | grep -v '^\s*$' | tail -14
arguments.description: Test diagnostics opt-out and re-enable in compiled TUI
